11910:
A parasite is a living thing that survives by feeding off another living thing — without giving anything back in return, and often while causing harm in the process.

The living thing being fed off is called the host. The relationship is completely one-sided: the parasite wins, the host loses.

Think of it like an uninvited guest who moves into your home, eats your food, drains your energy, and makes you sick — all while contributing nothing and having no intention of ever leaving.
The Three Rules of a Parasite

For something to be a true parasite, three things must be happening at the same time:

1. It lives on or inside another organism. The parasite doesn't just visit — it makes the host its permanent home or its source of survival.

2. It takes something from the host. Usually food, blood, nutrients, or energy.

3. It harms the host. This is the key detail that separates a parasite from other relationships. The host suffers — it may be weakened, made ill, or even killed over time.
Two Kinds of Parasites (by where they live)

Parasites that live inside the host are called endoparasites. Tapeworms, for example, live inside an animal's intestines and absorb digested nutrients directly, stealing food that the host's body was supposed to use. Malaria-causing parasites live inside red blood cells.

Parasites that live on the outside of the host are called ectoparasites. Fleas, ticks, and lice are classic examples. They sit on the skin or in the fur, bite through, and drink blood. You can actually see them — unlike the hidden ones inside.

Nature has many relationships between two different organisms, and it's easy to confuse them. Here's how parasitism stands apart:

In a mutual relationship, both sides benefit. Bees drink nectar from flowers, but in doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower — helping the flower reproduce. Both win.

In a commensal relationship, one side benefits and the other side is simply unaffected — neither helped nor harmed. Barnacles attaching to a whale get a free ride and access to food-rich waters; the whale doesn't notice or care.

In parasitism, one side benefits and the other side is genuinely harmed. There is no balance, no trade, no courtesy. The host pays the price simply by existing near the parasite.
The Parasite's Strategy: Don't Kill the Host (Usually)

Here's something fascinating and important: most parasites are not trying to kill their host. A dead host means no more food and shelter. So parasites tend to exploit just enough — weakening the host, draining it slowly, reducing its strength and immune system — but keeping it alive long enough to keep feeding off it.

This is actually what makes parasites more dangerous than many predators. A lion kills its prey quickly. A parasite may drain its host for years.

That said, some parasites do eventually kill their hosts, either because they multiply too aggressively, or because killing the host is actually part of how they spread to the next host.

The word "parasite" is also widely used to describe people, not just organisms. When someone calls a person a parasite, they mean that this person lives off others — taking money, resources, time, or effort from people around them without contributing anything meaningful in return.

For example: a person who constantly borrows money and never repays it, never works, relies entirely on others' generosity, and shows no intention of ever becoming self-sufficient might be called a parasite.

This is a harsh and insulting label when used about a person, but it accurately captures the same core idea: one-sided taking, at another's expense.
A Few Memorable Examples to Lock It In

• A tapeworm inside a dog's intestine is a parasite. It eats the dog's food, the dog loses nutrients, becomes thin and weak.
  • A tick on a deer is a parasite. It buries its head into the skin, drinks blood, and can transmit diseases.
  • The cuckoo bird practices a kind of social parasitism — it lays its egg in another bird's nest. The other bird raises the cuckoo's chick, often at the expense of its own offspring.
  • The malaria parasite (Plasmodium) lives inside human red blood cells, destroys them, and causes the fever, chills, and fatigue we call malaria.

A parasite is any organism that lives on or in a host, takes what it needs to survive, and harms the host in the process — a relationship built entirely on one-sided exploitation.

Everything else about this word is just detail layered on top of that core truth.
11911: A parasol is a portable, umbrella-shaped device designed to block sunlight and provide shade. Think of it as a "sun umbrella" — its entire purpose is protection from the sun, not from rain.

A parasol is a canopy of fabric stretched over a frame of thin, rigid spokes, all attached to a central handle or pole. You hold it above your head (or it stands on its own) to cast a shadow over yourself or an area below it.
How It Differs from an Umbrella

This is important to understand clearly. A regular umbrella and a parasol look very similar, but they serve different purposes:

  • An umbrella is built to keep you dry. It is made from waterproof material and is designed for rain.
  • A parasol is built to keep you shaded. It is designed for the sun. It may not be waterproof at all.

In casual, everyday speech, people sometimes use the two words interchangeably — especially when talking about patio or garden shade structures. But technically, and in careful usage, a parasol is the sun-specific one.

A parasol can be small and handheld, or large and freestanding. Either way, the basic structure is:

  • A canopy — the wide, dome-shaped top made of fabric (often lightweight materials like silk, cotton, lace, nylon, or canvas, depending on the type)
  • A frame of thin spokes or ribs that hold the canopy open
  • A central pole or handle running through the middle

1. Handheld parasol
This is the smaller, personal kind — compact enough to carry in your hand or bag. It opens and closes just like a regular umbrella, using the same folding mechanism. You hold it over your head while walking outdoors to protect yourself from the sun.

Handheld parasols are often elegantly designed. Historically, they were a fashionable accessory — particularly popular among women in 18th- and 19th-century Europe as a symbol of refinement. They came in rich colors with decorative details like lace trimmings and painted fabric.

Even today, handheld parasols are widely used across many parts of Asia (Japan, China, South Korea, India, and Southeast Asian countries) for practical UV protection. In Japan especially, using a parasol while walking outdoors on a sunny day is completely normal and common for both style and sun safety.

2. Garden or patio parasol
This is the large, freestanding kind — the tall, wide umbrella you see shading outdoor café tables, beach loungers, poolside areas, or garden seating. This type is not carried; instead, it has a long pole that either goes into the ground directly or fits through a hole in the center of a table.

Garden parasols are big enough to shade multiple people sitting beneath them. They can usually be tilted to adjust the angle of shade as the sun moves across the sky. You'll see them at outdoor restaurants, resorts, and in people's backyards.
Who Uses a Parasol and Why

People use parasols to:

  • Block UV rays — prolonged sun exposure causes sunburn and skin damage; a parasol provides a physical barrier
  • Stay cool — shade from a parasol can meaningfully reduce how hot you feel while outdoors
  • Fashion and style — especially the handheld variety, which has a long tradition as a stylish accessory
  • Ceremonial purposes — in many cultures (parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia), large, decorative parasols are used in religious ceremonies, royal processions, and cultural rituals as symbols of status, honor, or spiritual protection

Beyond the physical object, "parasol" is sometimes used loosely or figuratively to describe anything canopy-like that provides covering from above. For example, a large tree with wide-spreading branches might poetically be described as forming a natural parasol over a path.

The word is also used in biology — certain organisms (like some species of mushrooms or jellyfish) whose shape resembles an open parasol are sometimes described using this word, either literally or in their common names (e.g., "parasol mushroom").
Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture yourself on a hot, sunny afternoon. You're outdoors, squinting in the bright sunlight. You open a compact, fabric umbrella — but instead of rain falling on it, the sun beats down on it from above while you walk comfortably in its cool shadow below. That object in your hand is a parasol.
11912: A paratrooper is a soldier who is trained to jump out of an aircraft with a parachute and land in a combat zone to fight.

Think of a regular soldier. They usually travel to a battlefield by walking, driving in a vehicle, or sailing on a ship. A paratrooper does something very different — they fly over the battlefield in an aircraft (almost always a military plane or helicopter), jump out at a great height, and float down to the ground using a parachute — a large, dome-shaped canopy that opens up above them and slows their fall so they land safely.

Once on the ground, they fight just like any other soldier. The "para" in the word refers to parachute, and "trooper" is simply another word for soldier. So a paratrooper is literally a parachute soldier.
Why does this method of warfare exist?

Imagine a bridge deep inside enemy territory, or an airfield behind enemy lines — places that normal ground soldiers can't easily reach quickly because roads are controlled by the enemy or the terrain is too difficult. A paratrooper can bypass all of that. The aircraft flies over the obstacle, the paratroopers jump, and they arrive directly at the target — often taking the enemy by complete surprise.

This makes paratroopers extremely useful for:

  • Surprise attacks — enemies rarely expect soldiers to drop from the sky.
  • Capturing key positions — bridges, airfields, command posts — before the main army arrives.
  • Cutting off enemy escape routes — landing behind enemy lines to block retreating forces.
  • Raids — quick, precise operations to destroy something or rescue someone.
What makes a paratrooper different from a regular soldier?

Three things set them apart:

1. Specialized training. Becoming a paratrooper requires completing a demanding course (often called airborne school or jump school) where soldiers learn how to exit a moving aircraft safely, control their body during the fall, steer the parachute, and land without injuring themselves. Landing with a full load of equipment is actually quite hard — a poor landing can break ankles or legs, so the technique is drilled repeatedly.

2. They must be self-sufficient. When paratroopers land, they are often alone or in small groups, deep in enemy territory, with no immediate support. They carry everything they need — weapons, ammunition, food, medical supplies — on their bodies when they jump. This is why they are trained to be mentally tough and capable of making quick decisions independently.

3. They travel light but fight heavy. Because they carry everything on their backs (you can only bring what you can strap to yourself before jumping), paratroopers cannot bring heavy weapons like tanks or large artillery in a standard jump. However, modern militaries have solved this partially by airdropping heavier equipment in separate cargo loads — sometimes even driving light vehicles out of aircraft on large platforms.
The jump itself — what actually happens?

Paratroopers don't simply walk to the door of a plane and leap. There is a strict process:

  • The soldiers stand in a line inside the aircraft, hooked to a static line — a cable running along the ceiling of the plane. When a soldier jumps, this line automatically pulls their parachute open, so they don't have to pull a cord themselves. This is the most common method for military jumps.
  • A light signals them. When it turns green, they exit the aircraft one by one — fast — within seconds of each other. This is so the whole group lands close together rather than scattered across miles.
  • They fall for a moment, the parachute deploys, and they drift down — usually from an altitude low enough that they reach the ground in under a minute, giving enemy anti-aircraft guns less time to fire at them.
  • Upon landing, they immediately shed their parachute (it becomes dead weight and can tangle), orient themselves, find their fellow soldiers, and move to the objective.

Paratroopers are generally regarded as elite — meaning among the best and most capable soldiers in any military. The physical and psychological demands of their training weed out those who cannot handle it. Many armies around the world have famous airborne (paratrooper) units known for their toughness and discipline, such as the American 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions, the British Parachute Regiment, and the French Foreign Legion's parachute units.

The word airborne is very closely related — you will often see paratroopers described as "airborne troops." Airborne simply means "delivered to the battlefield through the air," and paratroopers are the most common type of airborne soldier.
How a paratrooper is different from other air-delivered soldiers

It is worth knowing that not all soldiers who arrive by air are paratroopers:

  • Air assault troops (like those arriving by helicopter) are not paratroopers — they land inside the helicopter or rappel down ropes; they do not jump with parachutes.
  • Paratroopers specifically jump and use parachutes. That distinction is what defines them.

You will most commonly encounter the word "paratrooper" in:

  • History and war documentaries — the D-Day landings of World War II (June 6, 1944) are among the most famous paratrooper operations ever, when thousands of Allied paratroopers jumped into Nazi-occupied France the night before the beach landings.
  • News reports about military operations.
  • Books, films, and video games set in military contexts.

When someone calls a soldier a paratrooper, you now know exactly what that means: a highly trained, airborne soldier who jumps from aircraft, parachutes into combat zones, and is capable of operating independently in dangerous, often behind-enemy-lines situations.
11913:
To parboil something means to partially cook it in boiling water, then stop before it is fully done. You pull it out of the water while it is still somewhat raw inside, and then finish cooking it later using a different method — like roasting, grilling, frying, or baking.

Think of parboiling as the first step of a two-step cooking process. The boiling water does some of the work, and then a second cooking method finishes the job.

Imagine you want to grill chicken pieces. If you throw raw chicken straight onto the grill, the outside chars and burns before the inside is cooked through. But if you parboil the chicken first — drop it into boiling water for, say, 10–15 minutes — the inside gets a head start on cooking. Now when you place it on the grill, you only need a short time to crisp and char the outside beautifully, and you can be confident the inside is safe and fully done.

The boiling did the hard work. The grill did the finishing.

Parboiling serves several very practical purposes:

1. To speed up total cooking time.
Since the food is already partway cooked, the second cooking method (grilling, roasting, frying) takes much less time. This is especially useful when dealing with dense, thick foods that take a long time to cook through.

2. To get better results from the second cooking method.
Some cooking methods — like roasting or frying — are great at creating crispy, golden, flavorful surfaces, but they are not efficient at cooking food all the way through quickly. Parboiling handles the inside; roasting/frying handles the outside. The result is often much better than doing either method alone.

3. To make the surface cook more evenly.
When you parboil something and then roast or fry it, the outside tends to become more uniformly golden and crispy, rather than having some parts overcooked and others undercooked.

4. To remove impurities or reduce strong flavors.
With some meats (especially bones and tougher cuts), parboiling draws out blood, impurities, and excess fat into the water, which you then discard. This is common when making clean, clear broths or soups.

5. To soften food slightly before further preparation.
Sometimes you need food to be pliable or slightly soft before you can handle or stuff it — for instance, parboiling cabbage leaves makes them flexible and easy to wrap around a filling.

Here are common real-life situations where parboiling is used:

  • Potatoes for roasting: You parboil potato chunks for about 10 minutes, drain them, then roast them in the oven. The parboiling makes the inside soft and fluffy while the oven crisps the outside to a beautiful golden crust. This is the classic secret behind truly crispy roast potatoes.
  • Ribs for grilling or baking: Pork ribs are parboiled first to tenderize the meat and remove some of the fat, then grilled or baked to caramelize the sauce and create a charred, sticky finish.
  • Chicken for grilling: As described above, parboiling prevents the common problem of burnt outside + raw inside on the grill.
  • Vegetables for stir-frying: Dense vegetables like broccoli, carrots, or green beans are sometimes parboiled briefly (just 2–3 minutes) so they cook quickly in the hot wok without staying raw in the middle.
  • Sausages: Sausages are often parboiled before pan-frying or grilling so the inside cooks fully without the casing splitting or the outside burning.
  • Rice (commercially): You may have seen the term "parboiled rice" on packets in a store. This refers to rice that has been partially boiled while still in its husk during processing. It cooks faster, holds its shape better, and is nutritionally richer than regular white rice.
How Parboiling Differs From Regular Boiling

This is an important distinction:

ConceptWhat it means
BoilingCooking food in boiling water until it is fully cooked and ready to eat.
ParboilingCooking food in boiling water until it is only partially cooked, then stopping and finishing it with another method.

With regular boiling, the pot is the only cooking method, and the food comes out ready to serve. With parboiling, the pot is just the first step — the food is not ready to eat after parboiling. It still needs more cooking.

• Partial, not complete. Parboiling never fully cooks the food. It's always a halfway step.
  • Always followed by another cooking method. You parboil in order to then grill, roast, fry, or bake.
  • The time in the boiling water is shorter than it would be for full boiling. You take the food out early, on purpose.
  • The boiling water is usually discarded. Unlike making soup where the water becomes broth, the water used for parboiling is typically poured away.
  • It is not the same as blanching. Blanching is a similar technique where food is plunged into boiling water for a very short time (sometimes just seconds to a couple of minutes) and then immediately cooled in ice water to stop cooking altogether — usually done just to brighten color, soften slightly, or preserve. Parboiling goes further and cooks the food more substantially, and there's no ice water stop — the food continues cooking via the second method.
To parboil is to boil food partially — just enough to give it a head start — before finishing it with a different cooking method like grilling, roasting, or frying.
11914: Before diving into the specific meanings, here is the central idea that connects all of them: a parcel is something singled out and treated as one complete, self-contained unit — whether it's a wrapped package, a piece of land, a batch of goods, or a group of things. Keep this idea in mind and every meaning will feel natural.
Meaning 1 — A wrapped package (the most everyday meaning)

When most people say "parcel," they mean something wrapped up, boxed, or bundled together so it can be carried, mailed, or handed over as a single item. It's the object that arrives at your door when you order something online, or the neatly tied bundle a person carries under their arm.

The key detail is that the items inside have been enclosed and prepared for transport — bound together into one neat unit.

"She received a parcel in the post."
"He wrapped the books into a neat parcel and left them at the door."

A parcel in this sense doesn't have to be mailed. If you bundle up food, cloth, or any objects and wrap them together, that bundle is a parcel too. The wrapping or bundling is what makes it a parcel — it becomes one thing rather than several loose things.
Meaning 2 — A piece or section of land

In property, real estate, law, and surveying, a parcel means a specific, defined piece of land — usually one that has been measured and marked out with clear boundaries.

Think of a large area of land divided into smaller sections on a map, each with its own number or reference. Each of those sections is a parcel.

"The government sold three parcels of land along the coastline."
"Each parcel of the property was listed separately in the legal documents."

This meaning shows up mainly in formal, legal, or property-related writing. The logic is the same as Meaning 1: just as a wrapped package singles out certain items from everything else, a parcel of land singles out a specific bounded piece from the wider landscape.
Meaning 3 — A quantity or batch of something (in trade and commerce)

In business, finance, and trade, a parcel refers to a specific quantity of goods, shares, or commodities being treated as one unit in a transaction.

"The company sold a parcel of 5,000 shares."
"A parcel of coffee beans arrived at the port for inspection."

Here, the word signals that these items — whether tea, grain, stocks, or any commodity — are being grouped and handled together as a single deal or lot. Again, the idea is a defined, self-contained unit.
Meaning 4 — A group or collection (often used dismissively)

Less common in everyday modern speech, but still used, parcel can mean a group or collection of people or things, often when the speaker is treating them as an undifferentiated mass — and sometimes with a slightly critical or dismissive tone.

"He called them a parcel of fools."
"She had a whole parcel of complaints."

This usage lumps people or things together the way items are lumped into a bundle. It often carries a hint of contempt or exasperation, but not always.

One of the most important uses of parcel as a noun is in the common phrase "part and parcel of something." This means an essential, inseparable element of something — not an optional add-on, but a core component that cannot be separated from the whole.

"Risk is part and parcel of starting a business." (= Risk is inherently built into starting a business — you cannot have one without the other.)
"Long hours are part and parcel of being a doctor."

The phrase is always followed by "of." It strongly emphasizes that the thing being described is not merely connected to the larger whole — it is built into it. If someone says X is "part and parcel of Y," they are saying you cannot truly have Y without X coming along with it.
How to tell which meaning is intended

The meaning almost always becomes clear from context:

  • Delivery, mail, post, wrap, box → it's a package.
  • Land, property, map, acres, real estate → it's a section of land.
  • Trade, shares, goods, cargo, lot → it's a batch or quantity.
  • People described dismissively, or a heap of problems → it's a group or collection.
  • "Part and parcel of..." → it means an essential component.
The thread that ties it all together

Every meaning of parcel shares one common idea: something bounded, defined, and treated as a single unit — singled out from a larger whole. A wrapped package is singled out from loose objects. A parcel of land is a defined piece singled out from a larger area. A parcel of shares is a specific batch singled out from the market. A parcel of people is a group lumped together and treated as one. Once you see this thread, the word will never confuse you regardless of the context.
11915: To parch means to make something extremely dry through intense heat — or to become extremely dry because of it.

"Parch" doesn't mean slightly dry. Think of dryness as a scale:

slightly dry → dry → very dry → parched

Parched is the extreme end. It suggests heat has aggressively sucked out all moisture, often leaving something cracked, shrivelled, or lifeless. It's the kind of dryness you see in cracked earth during a severe drought — not just dry, but beaten down and emptied by heat.
Two directions: doing it vs. experiencing it

1. Something parches something else (an outside force acts on an object):

  • The sun parched the fields.
  • Weeks without rain parched the farmland.
  • The desert wind parched his lips.

Here, the sun, drought, or wind is the cause — the "doer" — and it's making something else extremely dry.

2. Something parches on its own (the thing itself becomes extremely dry):

  • The soil parched as summer wore on.
  • His throat parched after hours without water.

Same meaning, just described from the object's perspective rather than naming what caused it.

You'll also see the word as "parching" to describe the cause of this dryness — "the parching heat of July" means a heat so fierce it dries and shrivels everything it touches.

Almost anything that can lose moisture through heat:

  • Land, earth, soil — The drought parched the valley.
  • Plants and crops — The harvest was lost when the crops parched in the heatwave.
  • Body parts: lips, throat, mouth, skin — Her lips were parched and cracked after the trek.
  • A whole person (through thirst) — which leads to the most common everyday use.

This is probably the most frequent use of the word in modern everyday speech. When someone says "I'm parched," they mean they are intensely, desperately thirsty — their mouth and throat feel completely dried out, and they urgently need water.

  • After two hours in the sun, I was absolutely parched.
  • The players came off the pitch parched and exhausted.

The logic is the same: just as heat dries out the earth until it cracks, your body can feel bone-dry when you haven't had water. "Parched" captures that feeling more vividly and urgently than simply saying "thirsty." It signals extreme thirst, not mild thirst.

There is an older, more specific meaning of "parch" found in food and agricultural contexts: to dry and lightly roast grains or seeds using dry heat — meaning no water, no oil, just direct dry heat.

  • They parched the corn before grinding it into flour.
  • Parched peas and parched maize are traditional foods prepared this way.

The method removes moisture and slightly toasts the grain, which preserves it and can intensify its flavour. The word is the same and the principle is identical — dry heat removes moisture — but here the drying is deliberate and purposeful (a cooking technique), not damage caused by nature.
The feel and weight of the word

"Parch" is a vivid, somewhat intense word. It carries connotations of scorching heat, harsh conditions, suffering, and urgent need. Writers use it to paint dramatic pictures of deserts, droughts, and physical exhaustion.

Notice the difference:

  • The land was dry. — neutral, unremarkable
  • The land was parched. — evocative; conjures cracked, lifeless terrain baked by a pitiless sun

When you choose "parch," you're signalling something beyond ordinary dryness. You're reaching for the extreme.

UseMeaning

To summarise cleanly:

  • Heat/sun/drought parches the land → it dries the land out severely.
  • Land/skin/throat parches → it becomes dangerously dry due to heat.
  • A person is parched → they are intensely thirsty.
  • To parch grain → to dry and lightly roast it over dry heat (specialised/traditional).

The thread through all of these is the same: intense, dry heat strips away moisture completely, leaving something desiccated, depleted, and desperate for water.
11916: Parched means extremely dry — so dry that it desperately needs water or moisture. The key word here is extremely. "Parched" is never used for something that is just slightly dry. It describes a serious, intense, almost painful lack of moisture. Think of the driest thing you can imagine — cracked desert ground under a blazing sun — and you're thinking of something parched.
The Two Main Ways "Parched" Is Used

1. To Describe Things and Places

When used for objects, land, or the environment, "parched" describes something that has lost almost all its moisture, usually because of intense heat or a long period without rain.

  • The parched earth cracked open under the summer heat.
  • The farmer looked sadly at the parched fields — not a drop of rain had fallen in weeks.
  • He ran his tongue over his parched lips, but there was no moisture left.
  • The hikers crossed a parched, dusty valley with no sign of water anywhere.

In these cases, you can almost see and feel the dryness. Parched land is not just a little dry — it is baked, cracked, and lifeless, starving for water. Parched lips are not just chapped — they are extremely dry and uncomfortable.

2. To Describe a Person (Extremely Thirsty)

When used for a person, "parched" means desperately thirsty — so thirsty that you feel an urgent need for water right now. This comes from the same idea: just as land becomes parched from lack of water, a person becomes parched when their body is starving for water.

  • After running for an hour in the heat, I was absolutely parched.
  • "Could I have a glass of water, please? I'm parched!" she said.
  • The soldiers marched through the desert, parched and exhausted.

This usage is very common in everyday conversation. When someone says "I'm parched," it simply means "I am very, very thirsty."

This is the most important thing to understand about "parched": it is always an extreme state. It is not a mild or moderate dryness. Compare:

  • Dry → some moisture is missing.
  • Very dry → noticeably lacking in moisture.
  • Parched → so severely dry that water is desperately needed, almost like a cry for relief.

If you say the grass is dry, it might just need watering. If you say the grass is parched, you picture it brown, brittle, and dying.
What Causes Something to Be Parched?

The most common cause is heat — especially prolonged, intense heat like a drought, a desert, or a blazing summer. However, a lack of rain alone (even without heat) can parch the land over time. For a person, physical exertion, hot weather, illness, or simply not drinking enough water can leave them parched. Occasionally, non-heat causes apply too — a person might have a parched throat after talking for hours or after a fever.
What Does "Parched" Look and Feel Like?

This is a word loaded with sensory detail. It paints a vivid picture:

  • Visually: cracked ground, brown and withered plants, dusty landscapes, dry and flaky skin or lips.
  • To the touch: rough, brittle, crumbly — like something that would fall apart if it got any drier.
  • As a feeling: an urgent, uncomfortable, almost desperate thirst — a scratchy, dry sensation in the throat.

When writers use "parched," they are trying to make you feel that dryness, not just understand it intellectually.

You will very often see "parched" used alongside these words, which helps you recognize it in context:

  • Parched earth / land / soil / ground — extremely dry terrain.
  • Parched lips / throat — extremely dry body parts craving moisture.
  • Parched landscape / desert / fields — a dry, desolate environment.
  • Absolutely / completely parched — intensifiers used when describing a very thirsty person.

• Dry is neutral and general. Parched is extreme and urgent. Your hair can be "dry." A dying desert is "parched."
  • Thirsty (for people) is mild. Parched is intense. You might feel "thirsty" before lunch. After a long run in the heat with no water, you feel "parched."
  • Arid is a more technical or geographical word used mainly for climates and regions (an arid climate). "Parched" is more vivid and emotional, and can apply to small things like lips or a throat, not just whole regions.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Parched" is slightly literary and expressive. It is perfectly natural in everyday conversation ("I'm parched — let's grab a drink!"), but it also appears frequently in books, poetry, and descriptive writing because it paints such a powerful picture. When you use "parched," you are not just stating a fact — you are conveying urgency, discomfort, and a deep need for water. It has an almost emotional weight to it.

Parched = extremely dry (for things/places) OR extremely thirsty (for people). It always signals an intense, severe lack of moisture — never a mild one. It often involves heat as the cause and carries a sense of desperate need for water.
11917: Parchment is a thin, flat sheet made from the treated skin of an animal — most commonly a sheep, goat, or calf — that people historically used as a surface for writing. Think of it as nature's version of paper, invented long before paper existed.
What It Is and How It's Made

To make parchment, the animal's skin is first soaked in water to soften it. Then it is stretched tightly across a wooden frame, scraped smooth with a special blade to remove hair, fat, and uneven patches, and left to dry under tension. As it dries while being held tight, it becomes thin, flat, pale, and firm — a surface clean and smooth enough to write on with ink.

The result is not leather (leather is tanned, meaning chemically preserved; parchment is simply cleaned, stretched, and dried). Parchment has its own distinct character: it is stiffer and lighter in color than leather, with a somewhat stiff, papery, and slightly waxy feel.

Parchment is typically cream-colored, off-white, or yellowish — never bright white. It has an old, warm, slightly aged look even when new. In bright light, you can sometimes see faint shadows where veins ran through the animal's skin. This is completely natural and is actually a sign of genuine, high-quality parchment.

For well over a thousand years — from roughly ancient times through the Middle Ages — parchment was the writing material of choice across much of the world, especially in Europe and the Middle East. Paper as we know it hadn't reached those regions yet, and earlier materials like clay tablets or papyrus (made from a plant) had significant limitations. Parchment was superior in many ways:

  • It was durable. Real parchment can survive for centuries — even millennia — under the right conditions. This is why we still have ancient religious manuscripts, legal charters, and hand-copied books from over a thousand years ago.
  • It could be scraped clean and reused if needed. A surface that was erased and rewritten on is called a palimpsest — a fascinating quirk of parchment's nature.
  • It was flexible enough to fold and bind into books, making it ideal for the early codex (the book format we still use today).

Kings, governments, churches, and scholars used parchment for their most important documents — royal decrees, religious scriptures, land deeds, laws, and sacred texts. The Magna Carta, for example, was written on parchment.
The Three Main Senses of the Word

The word "parchment" is used in three overlapping senses today:

1. The raw writing material itself
This is the original meaning — the actual sheet of animal skin, as described above. You might encounter this sense in historical or literary contexts: "The monk carefully unrolled the parchment and began to read."

2. An important document or certificate
Because parchment was historically the material used for official, formal, and permanent documents, the word "parchment" eventually came to mean any such important document — even if it isn't written on animal skin at all. Diplomas, royal charters, deeds, and legal documents are all called "parchments" in this sense. This is a figurative or extended use of the word, but it is entirely standard.

For example: "He received his parchment after four years of study" simply means he received his diploma or degree certificate.

3. Paper made to look and feel like parchment
Today, a thick, slightly cream-colored, stiff paper that resembles traditional animal-skin parchment is also called parchment (or parchment paper). It is used for printing certificates, formal letters, wedding invitations, and legal documents — because the appearance gives a feeling of formality, tradition, and prestige, even though it is ordinary paper.

There is also a separate product known as parchment paper in cooking — a heat-resistant, non-stick paper used in baking to line trays and prevent food from sticking. This gets its name from a slight visual resemblance to traditional parchment, but it is chemically treated paper and has nothing to do with animal skin. This usage is worth knowing simply to avoid confusion when you encounter the term in a kitchen or recipe context.

You will often see the word vellum used alongside "parchment." Vellum is essentially a finer, higher-quality form of parchment made specifically from the skins of very young animals — newborn calves, lambs, or kids (baby goats). Because the skin of young animals is thinner, smoother, and finer in texture, vellum produces an even more delicate and beautiful writing surface. Historically, the most precious manuscripts and the most important royal documents were written on vellum, not ordinary parchment.

In casual modern usage, the two words are often used interchangeably. But technically, all vellum is parchment, while not all parchment is vellum.

SenseWhat It Means

To put it plainly:

  • Parchment is writing material made from animal skin, stretched and dried until smooth and thin.
  • By extension, it can mean any important formal document, regardless of what it's actually made of.
  • It can also refer to paper that looks like the original material — used for certificates and formal printing.
  • In kitchens, parchment paper is a heat-resistant baking liner, a very different product sharing only the name.

The unifying idea across all these senses is the same: something that carries the feel — literally or figuratively — of importance, permanence, and formality. That is what parchment has always represented.

A pardon is an act of official forgiveness — specifically, forgiveness that removes or cancels a punishment. It is not just any forgiveness between people; it is always granted by someone in a position of authority, and it has real, formal consequences.

Think of it this way: if someone in power says, "This person was found guilty of a crime, but I am choosing to forgive them and free them from the consequences of that crime" — that act, and the document or decision behind it, is called a pardon.
The Primary Meaning: A Legal/Official Pardon

This is the most important and most commonly used meaning of the word "pardon" as a noun.

A pardon is an official decision made by a high authority — such as a President, a Governor, a King, or a Queen — to forgive a person for a crime and release them from all or part of the punishment they were sentenced to face.

Example: The president granted a pardon to the prisoner who had spent ten years in jail.

Here, "pardon" refers to the official act of forgiveness itself.

What does a pardon actually do?

A pardon can do several things, depending on how it is issued:

  • It can free a person from prison, even before their sentence is complete.
  • It can remove fines or other penalties the person was ordered to pay or face.
  • It can restore rights that a person lost because of their conviction — for example, in many countries, criminals lose the right to vote or hold public office. A pardon can give those rights back.
  • It can clear a person's name — especially useful in cases where someone was wrongly convicted, or where the law under which they were convicted is later seen as unjust.

Who can grant a pardon?

A pardon must come from someone with the recognized authority to grant one. It cannot come from just anyone. Common examples:

  • In India, the President has the power to grant pardons for offenses against central (union) law, including those punishable by death. Governors of states can pardon offenses against state law.
  • In the United States, the President can pardon any federal crime. State governors can pardon state crimes.
  • In the United Kingdom, the King or Queen grants pardons, acting on the advice of ministers.

This authority is usually written into a country's constitution or laws.
A Crucial Distinction: What a Pardon Is NOT

This is very important for understanding the word precisely. A pardon is often confused with other legal concepts. Here is how it is different:

Pardon vs. Acquittal

An acquittal means the court found the person not guilty — in other words, "you did not commit the crime."

A pardon means "you committed the crime (or were convicted of it), but the punishment is forgiven."

So an acquittal says the person is innocent. A pardon says the person was found guilty, but they are forgiven. These are very different. A pardon does not say the person is innocent.

Pardon vs. Commutation

A commutation reduces a punishment but does not forgive the crime. For example, a death sentence might be commuted to life imprisonment — the punishment is reduced, but the person is still convicted and still being punished.

A pardon goes further: it forgives the crime entirely and removes the punishment altogether (or most of it).

Pardon vs. Amnesty

Amnesty is similar to a pardon, but it is usually granted to a large group of people at once — often for political crimes or in the context of war.

A pardon is typically granted to a specific individual.

1. Full Pardon

A full pardon completely forgives the crime and its consequences. It restores the person's civil rights and releases them from all penalties. This is the most complete form.

2. Conditional Pardon

A conditional pardon is granted only if the person meets certain conditions. For example, a person might receive a pardon on the condition that they leave the country, stay out of trouble, or complete community service. If they break the conditions, the pardon can be withdrawn.

3. Posthumous Pardon

A posthumous pardon is granted to someone who has already died. This is typically done to restore the reputation of a person who was wrongly convicted or treated unjustly during their lifetime.

Example: Alan Turing, the British mathematician and war hero who was chemically castrated for being gay — which was a crime at the time — received a posthumous pardon decades after his death, when the law was recognized as deeply unjust.

4. Preemptive (or Prospective) Pardon

Some authorities have the power to grant a pardon before a person has even been tried or convicted. This is called a preemptive or prospective pardon. It is controversial, but it has happened.

Example: In 1974, US President Gerald Ford granted a preemptive pardon to former President Richard Nixon for any crimes Nixon may have committed during the Watergate scandal — before Nixon was ever charged or tried.
An Important Nuance: Does a Pardon Mean Innocence?

No, it does not.

A pardon forgives punishment. It does not declare innocence. The conviction, in many cases, still remains on the record. The legal and historical record still says the person was found guilty — the pardon simply says that the punishment has been removed.

However, in some legal systems, a full pardon can come with the clearing of one's criminal record (sometimes called expungement), meaning the conviction is also wiped from official records. But this depends on the country and the specific terms of the pardon.

In less formal, everyday contexts, the word pardon as a noun can also mean a simple act of excusing someone for a minor offense or mistake — essentially, forgiveness at the personal level.

Example: "He bowed his head and asked for her pardon after accidentally bumping into her."

Here, "pardon" means the forgiveness he was requesting. However, this usage is less common today in everyday speech (we are more likely to say "forgiveness" or "apology" in casual conversation). You will mostly encounter this sense in older or more formal writing.

To bring it all together:

A pardon (noun) is an official act of forgiveness granted by a person in authority that forgives a crime and removes punishment. It does not say the person is innocent — it says the punishment is cancelled. It can be full or conditional, given to an individual while alive or posthumously, and sometimes even granted before a conviction. It is different from an acquittal (which means "not guilty"), a commutation (which only reduces punishment), and an amnesty (which is for groups, not individuals). In rare, more formal or literary usage, it can also mean personal forgiveness for a minor social offense.
11919:
To pardon someone means to choose not to hold something against them — to release them from blame, punishment, or resentment, even when a wrong has genuinely occurred.

The key idea embedded in "pardon" is this: the wrong is acknowledged, not denied. Something did happen. But the person in a position to punish or resent chooses instead to let it go.

1. In Everyday Life — Forgiving a Fault

When you pardon someone in a personal, human sense, you forgive them for a mistake, a rudeness, or an offense. You decide not to stay angry or hold a grudge.

  • "She pardoned her friend for forgetting her birthday."
  • "He couldn't bring himself to pardon his brother for the betrayal."

Here, pardoning is an act of grace. You had every right to be upset, but you choose to let it go.

2. In Law and Government — An Official Release from Punishment

This is one of the most important uses of the word. When a head of state — a president, a king, a governor — pardons someone, they officially cancel that person's legal punishment. The person may have been convicted of a crime, but the authority steps in and says: "This person will not serve this sentence."

  • "The president pardoned the soldier before he could be executed."
  • "After new evidence came to light, the governor pardoned the wrongfully convicted man."

This is a powerful, formal act. A crucial point to understand here: a pardon does not mean the person is declared innocent. It does not erase guilt or overturn a conviction (unless the legal system specifically says so). It simply lifts the punishment. The record of the crime may still exist — but the consequence is removed.

Think of it this way: a judge says "you are guilty and must serve ten years." A pardon says "you will not serve those ten years" — but it doesn't say "you didn't do it."

3. Social Politeness — "Pardon Me"

You use "pardon me" to politely excuse a small, socially awkward action — interrupting someone, accidentally bumping into them, passing in front of them, sneezing, or saying something that might have been rude.

  • "Pardon me for interrupting, but the meeting starts in two minutes."
  • "Oh, pardon me!" (said after bumping into a stranger)
  • "Pardon me for saying this, but I think you have the wrong address."

In this use, you are essentially asking the other person to excuse a minor inconvenience or offense — a small request for grace. It signals politeness and awareness of social norms.

4. "Pardon?" — Asking Someone to Repeat Themselves

When used alone as a question, "Pardon?" is a polite way of asking someone to say something again because you didn't hear or understand them.

  • "Pardon? Could you speak a little louder?"
  • "Pardon? I'm afraid I didn't catch that."

This is softer and more polite than saying "What?" or "Huh?" It signals respect for the other person while acknowledging you missed what they said.
The Common Thread Across All Uses

Whether you're forgiving a friend, releasing a prisoner from a sentence, excusing yourself after interrupting, or asking someone to repeat themselves — every use of "pardon" shares one idea:

A small or large act of grace, in which someone is released from a consequence, a judgment, or an awkwardness.

The word always carries a sense of one person extending leniency or consideration to another.

Understanding what makes "pardon" different from close words will sharpen your understanding significantly.

Pardon vs. Forgive:
Both involve letting go of a wrong. But forgive is emotional and internal — it's about releasing resentment from your heart. Pardon is more formal and external — it's about releasing someone from consequences or blame. A judge can pardon a criminal (a formal, official act) without personally forgiving them in their heart. A mother can forgive her child emotionally without formally pardoning any consequence. In casual everyday speech, people use them almost interchangeably — but in formal or legal language, "pardon" is the correct word.

Pardon vs. Excuse:
These are very close in the social sense. "Excuse me" and "pardon me" are both used for minor inconveniences. But "pardon" tends to feel slightly more formal and deliberate. If you bump into someone on the street, both work. But if you want to interrupt a formal meeting or address someone of higher status, "pardon me" feels more appropriate. "Excuse" is also often used to justify behaviour ("She excused her lateness by blaming traffic"), while "pardon" is not normally used that way.

Pardon vs. Acquit:
This distinction is legally critical. To acquit someone means a court has determined they are not guilty — they didn't commit the crime. To pardon someone means they may well have committed it, but they are being released from punishment anyway. These are fundamentally different outcomes. An acquittal says "innocent." A pardon says "guilty, but freed."

"Pardon" is a word that naturally leans toward the formal side. In very casual speech, people more often say "forgive," "let it go," or just "no worries." But "pardon" becomes the right word in formal writing, legal contexts, official situations, and polite social interactions where you want to sound respectful and measured.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

To pardon someone is to extend a deliberate act of mercy or leniency — to decide that a wrong, an offense, or an inconvenience will not be punished, resented, or held against a person. It can happen on a grand, official scale (a head of state releasing a prisoner) or on a small, human scale (asking someone to forgive you for bumping their shoulder). The word always implies that something happened, that the person pardoning has the standing to respond to it, and that they choose grace over consequence.
